longQuestions: (1) Persistent deficit — imports exceed exports; (2) Exports concentrated on a few items — cotton, textiles, rice, leather, sports and surgical goods; (3) Imports mainly of petroleum, machinery, chemicals, edible oil, vehicles and iron and steel.

(4) Shift from raw materials to manufactured exports; (5) Concentration of markets — USA, EU, China, UAE, Afghanistan; (6) Low value-added and low-quality exports; (7) Exports affected by world prices and quotas; (8) Most trade is by sea through Karachi and Port Qasim.

(9) Rising import bill due to oil prices and population growth; (10) Government's control through tariffs, licences and export incentives; (11) Growing trade with China under CPEC and free-trade agreements; (12) Dependence on remittances and loans to finance the trade deficit.

(1) Earning foreign exchange needed for development; (2) Import of machinery, technology and raw materials for industry; (3) Import of petroleum — the main source of energy; (4) Import of food items (edible oil, wheat in shortage years) and medicines.

(5) Market for surplus agricultural and industrial products; (6) Employment in export industries; (7) Industrialisation and economies of scale; (8) Government revenue from customs duties; (9) Repayment of foreign loans and interest.

(10) Consumers get variety of goods; (11) Improvement in quality through competition; (12) Friendly relations with other countries; (13) Help in defence needs; (14) Raises national income and the standard of living.

(1) Increase production of exportable goods — modern agriculture and industry; (2) Improve quality and standardisation to meet international standards; (3) Diversify exports — new products (IT, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals) and value addition to cotton.

(4) Find new markets — Africa, Central Asia, Latin America; trade agreements; (5) Reduce cost of production — cheap energy, modern machinery, skilled labour; (6) Export incentives — rebates, tax refunds, cheap export finance; (7) Trade fairs, exhibitions and commercial attachés abroad.

(1) Imports far exceed exports — large trade deficit; (2) Rising oil import bill; (3) Narrow export base dependent on textiles; (4) Low quality and high cost of exports; (5) Fall in world prices of our exports.

(6) Heavy repayment of foreign loans and interest; (7) Import of luxury goods; (8) Rapid population growth increasing demand for imports; (9) Energy shortages reducing exports; (10) Political instability and law-and-order problems; (11) Protectionism by developed countries.

(1) Increase exports through higher production, diversification, quality improvement and new markets; (2) Reduce unnecessary imports — high duties on luxury goods; (3) Import substitution — produce at home goods now imported (edible oil, machinery); (4) Develop local energy resources (hydel, coal, solar) to cut the oil bill.

(5) Encourage home remittances through banking channels; (6) Attract foreign direct investment; (7) Promote tourism; (8) Reduce foreign borrowing and use loans productively; (9) Realistic exchange rate; (10) Control smuggling and under-invoicing.

(11) Population control; (12) Austerity in government expenditure; (13) Trade agreements with neighbouring countries; (14) Political stability and good governance; (15) Development of IT and services exports.

SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation) was founded in Dhaka in December 1985; its secretariat is in Kathmandu. Members: Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, Maldives and Afghanistan (since 2007).

Objectives: (1) Promote the welfare and quality of life of the people of South Asia; (2) Accelerate economic growth, social progress and cultural development; (3) Promote self-reliance among member countries; (4) Mutual trust and understanding; (5) Cooperation in agriculture, trade, science, technology, transport, health and education.

(6) Expansion of regional trade — SAPTA (1995) and SAFTA (2006); (7) Cooperation with other developing countries and international organisations; (8) Joint efforts against poverty, terrorism, drugs and natural disasters; (9) Strengthen cooperation in international forums on common interests.

Positive effects: (1) Removal of textile quotas (2005) gave Pakistan access to world markets; (2) Lower tariffs abroad increase opportunities for exports; (3) Access to cheaper raw materials and machinery; (4) Foreign investment and technology transfer; (5) Competition improves efficiency and quality; (6) Dispute-settlement mechanism protects Pakistan's trade interests.

Negative effects: (1) Local industries face strong competition from cheap imports; (2) Pakistan must reduce its own tariffs, cutting government revenue; (3) Subsidies to agriculture and industry must be reduced; (4) TRIPS raises prices of medicines, seeds and software; (5) Strict quality, environmental and labour standards act as barriers; (6) Developed countries continue to subsidise agriculture, harming our farmers; (7) Trade deficit may increase.
The rate of exchange is the price of one currency in terms of another. Under a free (floating) system it is determined by demand for and supply of foreign exchange in the foreign exchange market.

Demand for foreign currency (e.g. dollars) comes from importers, those paying foreign loans and interest, students and tourists going abroad, and investors sending money abroad. Supply comes from exporters, foreign investors, remittances of overseas workers, tourists coming in, and foreign aid and loans.

Equilibrium: the rate settles where demand equals supply. If demand for dollars rises (more imports), the rupee depreciates; if supply rises (more exports/remittances), the rupee appreciates. Theories: the mint-par theory (gold standard), purchasing power parity theory (rate depends on relative price levels) and balance of payments theory. Under managed float the central bank intervenes by buying or selling foreign currency.

(5) Participation in international trade fairs and exhibitions; (6) Commercial attachés in embassies; (7) Free-trade and preferential-trade agreements (China, Sri Lanka, Malaysia, GSP Plus with the EU); (8) Devaluation/market-based exchange rate to make exports competitive; (9) Export awards and tax concessions to exporters.

(10) Development of new export products — IT, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals, halal food; (11) Improved infrastructure — ports, dry ports, Gwadar; (12) Quality-control and standards institutions; (13) Textile and strategic trade policy frameworks.
